newsitem.title: USA: Court dismisses charges vs Orange County officials.
newsitem.headline: Court dismisses charges vs Orange County officials.

text.p: A state appeals court has dismissed charges against two Orange County, Calif., supervisors accused of misconduct in connection with the county's bankruptcy, attorneys said.

A 4th District Court of Appeal panel dismissed all charges against county Board Chairman Roger Stanton and Supervisor William Steiner, who faced removal from office had the accusations been sustained by a jury.
"We're ecstatic," said Steiner's attorney, Allan Stokke. "We felt all along we were right. It is clearly a victory."
Last December, a county grand jury accused Stanton and Steiner of failing to oversee former county Treasurer Robert Citron and other county finance officials.
They were also accused of voting to issue county debt without making adequate inquiries into the need for the borrowings and whether the county could repay them.

"In a nutshell, the accusations assert Steiner and Stanton did a shoddy job of minding the store while Citron committed acts which plunged the county into bankruptcy," the panel said. The panel added, however, that "something more than neglect" was needed to constitute willful conduct.
"To adopt the district attorney's proposed negligence standard would have ominous public policy implications," the panel's opinion said.

"It would effectively make the district attorney a performance monitor of elected officials," the panel said, and would allow the district attorney to subject them to trial if "he deemed their performance to fall below that of the 'reasonable' public official."
Orange County filed for bankruptcy protection on Dec. 6, 1994, after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. The county emerged from bankruptcy in June.
Orange County's District Attorney could appeal the ruling to the California Supreme Court. The District Attorney could not be reached for immediate comment on his plans.
Earlier this month, a judge ordered Citron to spend one year in county jail and pay a $100,000 fine for his role in the county's bankruptcy, the largest municipal bankruptcy in U.S. history.
